title: The Keys of Hollowmere
subtitle: The Legend of Ser Aldric
teaser: Forty knights swore to stand between Hollowmere and the wolves. When the wolves came, the grand master sold them the keys to the town, and thirty-nine knights did as they were told.

sections.heading: I. Not One Dent
paragraphs: In thirty years of making armour for the Order of Bronze, Hedda the bronzesmith had never once seen a piece come back dented.
She made all of it, breastplates and crested helms and round shields, and every spring it came back from the chapter house to be polished without a scratch on it.

Her son did the polishing. Aldric started at seven, on an upturned bucket in the corner of the forge, and he knew the Order’s oath before he could read, because the knights sang it across the lane at every feast.
“Hollowmere at my back. The wolf at my face. Between them, my word. By oath, I stand.”

They had sworn it for four hundred years, since the winter the lake froze and wolves came across the ice. Forty knights met them at dawn and swore it with swords raised, and the story said the rising sun ran down their blades like water, and the wolves fled.
Nobody had seen the light since. Hedda said that was what the story was for: so nobody would ask why.
“Then why do you make it so good,” Aldric asked her once, holding up a breastplate he could see his face in, “if they never use it?”
She worked the bellows a while before she answered. “I make it for the one who means it. There’s bound to be one eventually. Law of averages.”

Grand Master Anselm came to the forge to be measured whenever his waist went out. He was silver-haired, with a voice like a church organ, and on a chain around his neck he wore the three bronze keys to the gate of Hollowmere, the Order’s oldest charge. He took a liking to the boy with the rag and asked to hear the oath.
“You sound as if you believe it,” Anselm said.
“I do, my lord.”
“Well,” said Anselm, amused. “Somebody ought to.”

At nineteen, Aldric was knighted, the first tradesman’s son in sixty years, mostly because it amused Anselm. Aldric didn’t care why. He said the oath on his knees in the chapter house, and he was the only one in the room who was listening.

Anselm taught him the Order’s salute: the greatsword raised straight up, hilt before your face, to whoever you are about to fight. “So the light knows where to find you,” he said, the way you tell a child about the moon.
Hedda made Aldric’s armour heavier than anyone’s, and didn’t say why.

sections.heading: II. Three Keys
paragraphs: The Wolf King came out of the north the autumn Aldric turned twenty-two, with ten thousand spears and a great wolf’s pelt across his shoulders.
Hollowmere stands on an island at the end of the lake, joined to the north shore by a long timber bridge. At the town end is the gatehouse, and in the gate are three bronze locks.
The grand masters met behind locked doors for two days. On the third evening Anselm walked across the bridge alone and came back without his chain.

That night he told the forty knights plainly, in the beautiful voice. The grand masters had knelt to the Wolf King and given him the keys. He would ride in at dawn. Every knight who stood aside would keep his life, his lands and his horse.
“It’s a good bargain,” Anselm said. “Better than we had any right to. Stand down.”
Thirty-nine knights looked at the floor.
“There are two thousand people in Hollowmere,” Aldric said.
“And ten thousand spears on the shore. Do your sums.” Anselm wasn’t angry. He looked old, and tired, and very sure. “It’s a song, boy. We sing it at dinner. I’m sorry nobody told you.”
“Between them, my word,” Aldric said. “You gave yours away, my lord. I’ve still got mine.”
He took his helm from its peg and walked out. Nobody came with him.
He let the iron portcullis drop behind the gate, jammed the windlass with a pike, and went through the town hammering on doors until every house was awake.

sections.heading: III. A Town Without Doors
paragraphs: Hollowmere had boats enough for two hundred people. Hedda solved the rest. She came up the gatehouse stair after midnight with soot on her face and a coil of rope over her shoulder.
“Doors float,” she said.

Before dawn every door in Hollowmere was off its hinges, the chapter house doors included, which nobody asked about. Lashed together with rope and bedsheets, they made rafts, and the town pushed off for the south shore, steering wide of the Hollow, the slow whirlpool at the heart of the lake that gave the town its name and its seal.

At dawn the Wolf King’s men came over the bridge with the keys. The keys worked perfectly. The great gate swung open, and behind it was the portcullis, and above that the murder holes, and in the murder holes, Aldric.

He held the gatehouse for a day and a night. He dropped its stones on them, then its furniture, then its roof beams. When they lit fires against the portcullis, he doused them from the well in the gatehouse floor. By midnight he had more dents than the whole Order had collected in four hundred years.
Out on the black water, the rafts went, and came back, and went again.
An hour before the second dawn, Hedda climbed the stair one last time.
“Last raft,” she said. “It’s our door. Come on.”
“If I leave the gate, they’re on the quay before you’ve cast off.”
“Aldric.”
“I can’t, Mam.”

She looked at him by the light of the fires below: at the helm she had made, dented to the crest, and the breastplate beaten in from collar to belt. She laid her palm flat on the worst of the dents, the way she tested a piece for true.
“Well,” she said. “About time.”
Then she went down and pushed off on her own front door, the last raft out of Hollowmere. He watched it until he couldn’t tell it from the water.
He was holding the gate for two thousand people. He was honest enough to know he was holding it for one.

sections.heading: IV. The Bridge at Dawn
paragraphs: By the second dawn the last raft was a speck off the south shore, and the gatehouse had run out of stones, beams and furniture. Aldric had run out of most things too.

The lake was wide, but not wide enough. Sooner or later the Wolf King would ride round it. So Aldric raised the portcullis, walked out onto the bridge in front of ten thousand spears, and called for the king.
The Wolf King came, because a king who refuses a challenge in front of his army does not stay king for long. He was older than Aldric expected, and bigger, with an axe as long as a man.
“Your masters sold me this town for their lives,” he said. “Knelt on these planks to do it. What will you sell it for?”
“It isn’t mine to sell,” Aldric said. “It wasn’t theirs either.”
He raised his greatsword straight up, hilt before his face, in the salute Anselm had taught him like a bedtime story.
The Wolf King laughed. Then the sun cleared the hills, and the light came down.

Not a glint. A column of it, white and gold, out of a clear sky onto the blade, as if it had been looking for that sword for four hundred years. Both armies saw it. On the south shore, two thousand people standing among their beached doors saw it.
The Wolf King stopped laughing. Then he came on anyway, because he was a brave man.

Aldric had been fighting for a day and a night, and every blow of the axe knocked him down. The third time, he went to one knee and stayed there, his sword arm numb to the shoulder. The Wolf King stood over him with the axe raised.
“Kneel, then,” he said, not unkindly. “Your masters did. Nobody will think less of you.”
Aldric thought of a woman on a door on the far shore, watching.
“By oath,” he said, “I stand.”
He stood, and the sword came up with him, under the axe, through the wolf’s pelt and into the king.
The Wolf King sat down heavily against the rail.
“They’ll never forgive you for this,” he said. “Your masters.” He fumbled at the clasp at his throat. “Take the cloak. They’ll take everything else.”
By noon there was not a spear left on the north shore, and Hollowmere was coming home across the lake on its doors.

The Wolf King was right. That evening the grand masters walked back from his empty camp, and Anselm stood on the steps of the chapter house, which had no doors, and cast Aldric out of the Order for defying a lawful command. His name was struck from the roll and his spurs taken. Then Anselm held out his hand for the keys.
Aldric had taken them from the Wolf King’s belt. He looked at the hand for a long moment. Then he turned and gave them to his mother.

Hedda melted them down that night with every bronze buckle the town could spare, and by morning they were a round shield. The town council struck it with Hollowmere’s whirlpool seal and hung it on his arm in front of everyone.
“There,” Hedda said. “Now nobody can sell them again.”

sections.heading: V. Oath of Bronze
paragraphs: By the Order’s rules he isn’t a knight. Hollowmere has never called him anything but Ser Aldric.

He wears the helm Hedda made, because she says it was hers to give and isn’t theirs to take, and the Wolf King’s pelt on his shoulders, because a dying man asked him to. Hollowmere’s gate has no keys anymore. They’re on his arm.

The Order of Bronze still has its chapter house, with new doors, and thirty-nine knights, and nobody in Hollowmere will sell them bread. Anselm is very old now. They say that when the knights sing the oath on feast days, his voice stops just before the last line.

Aldric fights in the duelling rings because they are the one place where a man gives his word out loud in front of a crowd, and keeps it or breaks it where everyone can see. He grew up listening to men sing words they didn’t mean. Somewhere in every crowd there’s a child on an upturned bucket who still believes them. He wants that child to see one who meant it.

Before every bout he raises his greatsword to his opponent, hilt before his face, the salute the Order taught him and never once used. And the light comes down. It has never failed him. He has never once been sure it would.
Hedda says it’s simple. The light was promised to whoever kept the oath. It just had a long wait for anyone to collect.
Then he lowers the blade, sets the shield, and says the last line of an oath that thirty-nine knights still sing at dinner.
“By oath, I stand.”

Every winter he brings the shield home to the forge. It is the most dented piece of bronze in the world. Hedda’s eyes are going, so she reads it with her fingers, the way she tests a piece for true, and every year he asks whether she’d like to hammer the dents out.
“Leave them,” she says. “I waited thirty years for those.”
